title: Search console after a redesign
excerpt: After a redesign, watch the queries that used to bring people, the pages that fell, and the redirects. Do not redesign again out of nerves in the first month.
alt: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky. The tall buildings seen from below fit a piece about looking up at the same pages after a redesign, without tearing them down again.
caption: Look up at the same structure before you rebuild it. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should you watch in Search Console after a redesign?
faqs.answer: The queries that used to bring people, the pages that lost clicks or impressions, and the redirects from old URLs. Compare a few weeks before launch with a few weeks after, once data exists. A drop concentrated on one URL usually means that page moved, got thinner, or is blocked. A drop across everything may be a crawl, an index, or a measurement lag.

faqs.question: How soon should you redesign again if numbers fall?
faqs.answer: Not in the first month, out of nerves. Google's title-link documentation notes that recrawl and reprocessing can take days to weeks, so look for broken redirects and missing pages immediately. Those are fixes, not a new design. Change the design again only when a specific page fails a specific query.

faqs.question: Which drops deserve a real response?
faqs.answer: Ones you can explain. Google's helpful-content guidance suggests auditing drops by which pages were hit and which searches. A merged page should pass people through a redirect, and a page you still care about needs a clearer title and a clearer answer if it no longer matches its query. A vague slump, with the site still indexed, is a reason to watch.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Watch the queries that used to bring people, the pages that fell, and the redirects. That is the job of search console after redesign. Do not redesign again out of nerves in the first month. The new site needs time to be crawled, and you need time to tell a broken redirect from a ordinary fluctuation.

Search Console is the record of how Google sees the site: which queries, which pages, which coverage problems. It is not a mood. Read it against the list of URLs you changed. The redesign already happened. This pass is how you find out whether the moves you made are the moves visitors now take.

## What you can see, and when

Open the performance report and compare a period before launch with a period after, of similar length, once the after period exists. Look at queries and at pages. Clicks, impressions, and the queries themselves matter more, at first, than a single average position. Averages hide a page that disappeared.

Coverage, or the pages report that shows indexing, tells you whether the new URLs are known and whether the old ones are dropping out. A redesign that ships on Friday will not have a full picture on Monday. Google's documentation on title links notes that the system has to recrawl and reprocess a page to notice title changes, and that this can take a few days to a few weeks. Treat that as the pace for other on-page changes too. Inspect an important URL if you need to know whether this specific page has been seen. Do not refresh the whole information architecture because a chart has not moved yet.

Keep a copy of the before data. Export the top queries and the top pages from the month before launch, and save it with the project. You will not remember the list. The report will move on. The export is how you know what "used to" means. If you never had Search Console on the old site, start it now and be honest that you are watching forward, not comparing. Guessing the old traffic from memory is how teams invent a crisis.

## The queries that used to bring people

Sort the before export by clicks. Those queries are the demand you already earned. For each one that mattered, name the page that served it. After launch, check whether that query still shows, and whether the page that appears for it is the page you intended. A query that now lands on a thinner page, or on the homepage, is a content problem or a redirect problem. It is visible. It is fixable without a new visual concept.

Read the query as a question. If you removed the paragraph that answered it, because the new design wanted fewer words, put the answer back. A calmer layout can still hold a direct sentence. Cutting the only answer and then watching the query fall is cause and effect. Restore the answer in the new type, under a heading that states it.

Do not stuff the old query into the title to drag the chart back. Google's title-link guidance says keyword stuffing makes results look spammy, and that vague or boilerplate titles get rewritten. Write a title that describes the page. If the page is no longer about that query, let the query go, on purpose, and make sure the redirect or the new page serves the people who still arrive with that need. Intentional cuts are fine. Accidental ones are the leaks.

Brand queries should still find you. If your name now struggles, look at the homepage title, the indexability, and whether a staging site or a duplicate got indexed. That is an emergency of a different sort from a dip in a how-to article. Fix discovery of the front door before you debate the hero illustration.

## The pages that fell

Sort pages by the change in clicks. A single URL that collapsed usually has a story. It moved and the redirect is missing. It was merged and the new page does not cover the old ground. It is blocked, noindexed, or canonicalized to the wrong place. It now returns a soft success that is actually empty. Open the URL. Use the inspection tool. Look at the response, not only at the chart.

A cluster of pages that fell together often shares a template. The new article layout, the new project layout, the paginated work index. Check one of them thoroughly rather than tweaking ten. Titles, headings, internal links, and whether the text is in the HTML or painted in after a script. A marketing page that only fills in on the client will look empty to a crawler in a hurry. The offer belongs in the first response.

Some pages should fall. You deleted a thin offer, you combined duplicates, you removed a tag archive that never helped anyone. Mark those in the export so you do not "save" them. Google's helpful-content guidance suggests auditing drops by which pages were affected and for what searches, and it warns against adding or removing content mainly to seem fresh. Put a page back because a real query lost a real answer. Do not put a page back because a line on a chart dipped and you miss the old template.

Internal links are part of this picture. A page that is no longer linked from the homepage or the nav will fade even if the URL still works. If the page still matters, link it from a sentence in the new information architecture. A redesign that flattens the nav and orphans the library will show up as a slow loss on those URLs. Link the ones you mean to keep. Let the others go with a redirect to the best remaining page, not to a generic home for everything.

## Redirects

Every URL you changed on purpose needs a permanent redirect to the closest new page. Not everything to the homepage. A person, and a crawler, who asks for the old pricing article should land on the page that now discusses pricing. A map is the deliverable. Old path, new path, one hop.

Check the map against the before export. The top pages must be on it. Then test them as requests, not as theory. A redirect that chains through three addresses, or that loops, or that lands on a 404, is unfinished. A redirect that points at a URL which itself redirects is a cleanup task for the same week, not a later sprint. Chains are how a simple move becomes a slow, fragile one.

Watch the not-found report if you have it, or the log of 404s, for URLs that the map missed. Partners, old ads, and email still point at the past. Add the redirect when a real URL shows up more than once. Do not redirect your entire history at the homepage to make the report quiet. That hides the miss and gives the visitor a page they did not ask for.

Staging hosts, test subdomains, and parameterized duplicates should not be in the index. A redesign is when they leak, because someone linked a preview. Canonical tags and passwords or a noindex on anything that is not the public site are part of launch, and they are part of the week-after check. Inspection will show you if a stray host is the one Google kept.

## The first month

Make a short list of checks and stop. Week one: redirects, index coverage on the key templates, homepage and offer titles, a manual look at the top ten old URLs. Week two and three: the query export against the new pages, and any page that lost the answer it used to give. Week four: decide what is a real regression. That decision should name a URL and a query. "Traffic feels down" is not a decision.

Do not open a new redesign in that month. Visual anxiety is normal. The team is tired of the new type because they have stared at it. Buyers are not. Changing the structure again resets the crawl and destroys the comparison you are trying to read. Fix bugs. Restore a sentence. Correct a title. Leave the system alone unless it is actually broken.

Annotate the launch date in your notes so later readers know why the chart kinks. If you also changed a price, a season, or a campaign, write that down too. Search Console will not separate those causes for you. A dip that matches the end of a paid push is not a failure of the type system. Do not pay for a rebuild to explain a calendar event.

Share the reading with the founder in plain language. Which queries still land. Which page needs a paragraph back. Which redirect was missing and is now in. A studio that disappears after launch leaves the founder alone with a chart. The chart is more useful as a shared review than as a scoreboard.

## What a fix looks like

A fix is specific. Restore the heading that matched the query, in the new design. Point the old URL at the new one. Remove a noindex you left on during the build. Put the text back in the HTML. Ask for indexing on the few URLs that matter, then wait. A pile of unstructured edits, made because the line went down, will give you nothing to learn next time.

Titles deserve a careful pass, not a frantic one. Each page's title should describe that page, in the language of the page, without boilerplate repeated so heavily that every result looks the same. Google may still rewrite a title. If the rewrite is clearer, learn from it. If the rewrite is wrong because the heading on the page is wrong, fix the heading. The documentation lists the sources the system uses, including the visible title and the headings. Make those agree.

Leave a note in the repository: what the before export showed, what you changed, what you refused to change. The next redesign, a year from now, will start from that note instead of from fear. The goal is a site that can evolve without amnesia.

Hanabi treats the redirect map and the before-and-after queries as part of shipping, not as an optional analytics engagement. The design can be new. The paths people already use should not be careless.

If you are about to launch and you want that map to be part of the work, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the list of URLs that already earn visits. The redesign should know their names.

Once the pages are stable, the words people see in search still have to earn the click. [Writing meta descriptions people will click](/blog/writing-meta-descriptions-people-will-click) is the next piece, because a sound redirect into a vague result still loses the visit at the listing.
